extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical moral philosophy / ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and definitions of voluntary/involuntary action, moral choice, deliberation, wish, formation of virtue, and the nature of courage from an Aristotelian ethics perspective. Focuses on conceptual distinctions, examples, and implications for praise, blame, and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of involuntary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary actions are those done either on compulsion or by reason of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds: (1) compulsory (origination external to agent), and (2) ignorance-caused. This distinction is necessary for assigning praise and blame and for legislators deciding honours and punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of compulsory action
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is compulsory when the origination is external to the agent and the agent contributes nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: being carried by the wind, being moved by men who have power over your person. If the agent contributes to the motion (e.g., moving one's limbs), the action is not properly compulsory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed/partly voluntary actions (duress and emergency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions under threats (e.g., ordered to commit a base act to save loved ones) or emergency acts (throwing goods overboard in a storm) are mixed but most like voluntary actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acts are choice-worthy at the time given the circumstances; origination may rest in the agent (movement of limbs), so they are treated as voluntary though abstractly one might not choose them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness determined at time of action
rubrics_metrics.description: An action must be denominated voluntary or involuntary at the time of doing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment depends on the facts at the moment of action (origination, awareness), not on abstract or retrospective judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and blame tied to voluntariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise and blame arise with voluntary actions; for involuntary actions allowance or compassion is often made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: men are sometimes praised for enduring disgrace to secure honourable ends; in other cases allowance is made when human endurance is overstrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance-caused action and regret criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every action caused by ignorance is involuntary; only that which is attended with pain and remorse is properly involuntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agent lacks regret, the action is 'not-voluntary' rather than involuntary. Distinguish acting 'because of' ignorance from acting 'with' ignorance (e.g., drunk or angry persons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting because of ignorance vs with ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between actions caused by ignorance and actions performed in a state of ignorance (e.g., drunkenness or anger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We don't ordinarily assign ignorance as the cause for actions of the drunken or angry; the state (drunkenness/anger) is the cause, even if the action is performed without full knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of particulars vs ignorance of principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of particular details that constitute the action can make it involuntary, whereas ignorance of principle (moral ignorance) generally constitutes depravity and does not excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only ignorance about particulars (who, what, with what instrument, result, how) invites compassion; ignorance of what one ought to do (principles) is blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of particulars relevant to voluntariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular details relevant to whether an action is involuntary include who acts, what he is doing, with respect to what, sometimes with what instrument, the result, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignorance in any of these particulars can render an action involuntary, especially ignorance regarding the particulars in which the action consists and the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of voluntary action
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary action is one whose origination is in the agent, the agent being aware of the particular details in which the action consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntariness requires both origination in the agent (he can do or not do) and awareness of particulars; actions from anger or lust are not thereby automatically involuntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of anger/lust as involuntariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done from anger or lust are not properly classed as involuntary simply because they stem from passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anger or lust are motives, the action can still be voluntary; otherwise only animals or children would alone be capable of voluntary actions. Anger may sometimes be a duty; lust may aim at proper objects (health, learning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice distinguished from voluntary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice (prohairesis) is plainly voluntary but not co-extensive with voluntary action; it is voluntary that has passed through previous deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice involves reasoning and intellectual process; children and animals may act voluntarily but lack Moral Choice; sudden actions may be voluntary but not instances of Moral Choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation scope: objects and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation concerns matters that a sensible person would deliberate about: practical matters within one's power and not about ends, eternal truths, necessary events, chance, or exact sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We deliberate about means to ends, where there is some indefiniteness about how a given case will issue. Not about ends (physician doesn't deliberate whether to cure), not about trivial sensory details, nor about impossible or fortuitous matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation aims at means, not ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation investigates means to ends; Moral Choice is the selection of means after deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deliberating, one examines which means are possible, easiest, or most creditable; if only one means exists one analyses through to the first cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination of deliberation and origination in self
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation ends when the process of bringing origination up to the self is complete; the object of Moral Choice is that which after deliberation is preferred and rests with the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice is 'a grasping after something in our own power consequent upon deliberation' and is followed by the will's assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wish vs Choice: ends vs means and possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Wish has for its object the End; Choice is concerned with means to ends and with things believed possible through one's own agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wish may target impossible things (immortality) or things where one has no instrumental control; choice requires belief that one can be instrumental in procuring the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and vice are in our power (formation of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are habits formed by repeated voluntary acts; since doing and forbearing are in our power, forming good or bad character is in our power and thus voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One becomes virtuous or vicious through repeated actions; the origination of habits is voluntary even if the gradual formation may be less perceptible (like sickness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for self-caused ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance that is self-caused (e.g., drunkenness) is blameworthy and punished; people may be chastised for ignorance they could and should have prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: penalties doubled for the drunken; ignorance of legal regulations which are not hard to know is culpable. Neglect leading to bad character is itself voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between being unable now and being originally responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one no longer can change (e.g., a man become unjust or intemperate), he may have been originally voluntary in bringing himself into that state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past voluntary acts can ground present character; one may now be unable to change but was previously responsible for becoming such by voluntary actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage defined as a mean state
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage (bravery) is a mean state between fear and boldness in respect of right objects (primarily honourable danger) and is chosen and acted on as right reason directs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects of fear for the brave are the greatest (e.g., death) but specifically death in honourable circumstances (war). The brave act from honour and withstand what is fearful for the right motive, manner, and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rightness conditions for courage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Brave man is one who withstands danger for the right object, from the right motive, in the right manner, and at the right time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors include fearing too much (coward), fearing too little or being rash (excess confidence), and fearing wrong objects or at wrong times. Bravery is related to honor as motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limits of courage (when it applies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage properly applies where action can help oneself and where death would be honourable (e.g., in war); it does not properly apply to drowning or sickness where these requisites fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bravery differs by context: seamen may be fearless from experience, landsmen brave in war-like contexts. Courage involves readiness to act when something can be done to help oneself and when death is honourable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species/variants of courage
rubrics_metrics.description: There are related dispositions called 'courage' in common speech: civic courage (motivated by shame/honour), compelled service courage (from commanders' compulsion), and experience/skill-based bravery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic courage most closely resembles true courage because it arises from virtue and shame; courage under compulsion is lower, and experienced/skill-based display may resemble courage though it can fail when danger exceeds means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of excess and defect in courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess in confidence yields rashness (often a mixture of bravado and cowardice), defect in confidence yields cowardice (fearing wrong objects/times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rash persons are precipitous and may fail in real danger; cowards fear too much and lack proper confidence. The brave are composed before danger and quick in action.
